entities.summary:
Capelianus, a Roman provincial governor of Mauretania Caesariensis (modern Algeria), emerged as a pivotal military figure in 238 CE, the tumultuous 'Year of the Six Emperors.' Though his exact birth and death dates remain unrecorded, his actions profoundly influenced the succession crisis that engulfed the Roman Empire, ultimately contributing to the downfall of the Gordian dynasty and the continued instability of the barracks emperors. His loyalty to Emperor Maximinus Thrax placed him in direct opposition to the senatorial faction, whose support for the Gordians sparked a brief but bloody civil conflict in North Africa.

In early 238 CE, when Gordian I and his son Gordian II were proclaimed emperors in Africa Proconsularis, challenging the rule of Maximinus Thrax, Capelianus, as the governor of the neighboring province, marshaled his local forces. These included not only regular legionaries but also a significant contingent of seasoned veterans and local militias, many with personal grievances against the Gordians. Leading this army, Capelianus marched into Africa Proconsularis, clashing with Gordian II's hastily assembled forces near Carthage. The ensuing battle was a decisive victory for Capelianus, resulting in the overwhelming defeat and death of Gordian II. Upon receiving news of his son's demise, Gordian I, then 80 years old, committed suicide, bringing their brief reign to an abrupt and violent end.
